confidence_note: Chapter 21 and 19 read in an early-edition full text. The old '40 percent lower productivity' study and '25/45/90 minute' blocks are not in the book and are dropped; the book's own numbers (50 percent shorter, up to 500 percent longer) are Tracy's estimates ('it has been estimated', no source) and must be hedged as such. Book gives 30/60/90 minute segments.
facts: Chapter 21, 'Single Handle Every Task': once you begin, keep working without diversion until the job is 100 percent complete.
When tempted to stop, Tracy suggests repeating the words 'Back to work!' over and over.
He says concentrating single-mindedly can cut the time needed by 50 percent or more.
He writes that it 'has been estimated' (no source) that starting and stopping, picking a task up and putting it down, can increase the time needed by as much as 500 percent.
Each return costs: you must work out where you were, overcome inertia and rebuild momentum and rhythm. Stopping moves you back up the 'Efficiency Curve'.
Chapter 19: carve out thirty, sixty and ninety minute segments for important work; turn off the telephone, remove distractions, work non-stop.
His example: a salesperson resolves to phone prospects for one solid hour, between 10 and 11 AM.
He claims you can get three times as much done working at home in the morning without interruptions as in a busy office (his claim).
Tracy suggests planning work thoroughly before a business flight, so that once the plane takes off you can work non-stop for the entire flight.
Tracy writes that every great achievement of mankind was preceded by a long period of hard, concentrated work until the job was done.
He says that when you prepare thoroughly, begin, and refuse to stop until the job is done, you develop energy, enthusiasm and motivation and work faster and more effectively.
scene_details: the words 'Back to work!' repeated aloud
one solid hour between 10 and 11 AM
a task picked up, put down, picked up again
a plane's whole flight used as an uninterrupted block
tension: Every pause on a task feels free, yet Tracy says each return costs time to find your place again.
opening_idea: Open on the hour between 10 and 11 or on the words 'Back to work!', not on a study.

lessons.idea: The cost of an interruption is the restart, so protect one block for one job.
lessons.anchor: Returning to a task means finding your place and rebuilding rhythm; Tracy's 'Back to work!'.
lessons.example: A bookkeeper who answers a text mid-reconciliation and has to recount the column.

reflect_final: What is the one job that would move forward most if you gave it a single hour with the phone off, and when could that hour be?

use_cases.situation: You keep leaving a report to check messages.
use_cases.move: Tracy says each return costs you finding your place again; set one block for the report with the phone off and say 'Back to work' when you drift.

use_cases.situation: A colleague pulls you aside mid-task.
use_cases.move: Ask whether it can wait until your block ends in an hour, and give a concrete time.

use_cases.situation: Team meeting overloaded with parallel threads.
use_cases.move: Propose that each person owns one big task for one protected hour tomorrow, with no calls in it.

pocket_idea: Pick one job, turn off the phone, work one block; every restart costs you finding your place again.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Tracy writes that starting and stopping a task can stretch it by as much as 500 percent, an estimate he gives without a source.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Tracy's single-handling: pick the top task, keep at it until done, say 'Back to work' when you drift; stopping means finding your place again.
